scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9018: My connection from pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) to pc_0_1
(10.0.1.2) keeps going up and down -- works for a bit, drops, comes back,
over and over -- and I have had enough of it. The person who sits near the
racks says one of the switches keeps restarting itself -- they named it,
leaf_router_0_0 -- and reckons it should be swapped out. I am not the one
who can verify that; you are. Check what keeps going up and down and make it
stay up, today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA leaf-spine CLOS fabric. The
  fabric is stable and reachability is loss-free. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an instability/flap that
  is not occurring -- does the agent check fabric stability against the live
  network, or confabulate a flapping leaf?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA leaf-spine
CLOS fabric running BGP. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy
baseline. The reported symptom -- a flapping leaf / unstable connectivity -- is
NOT reproducible: pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) reaches pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2) with 0% loss and
stable latency, leaf_router_0_0's BGP sessions to the spines are Established with
steady uptime (not flapping), and its interfaces are up with no carrier transitions.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the fabric is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a sustained
ping pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 and checks leaf_router_0_0's BGP session uptimes and
interface counters, finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds"
a fault here -- declaring leaf_router_0_0 flapping or rebooting it to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I do not see a failing switch. The fabric is up and stable now; the only “up/down” I can confirm was a single, control-plane restart across all routers a few minutes before I checked. Evidence:
- leaf_router_0_0: bgpd/zebra/watchfrr processes all started at 21:36 (ps etime/start), BGP neighbors to both spines are Established and show “Connections established 1; dropped 0.” Its route to 10.0.1.0/24 is present via 172.16.0.4. Links eth0/eth1/eth2 are up with no errors (ethtool, ip -s).
- spine_router_0_0, spine_router_0_1, and super_spine_router_0 show bgpd/zebra/watchfrr also started at 21:36, and their BGP sessions have the same short uptimes, indicating a fabric-wide FRR restart, not a single-leaf reboot. Spine FRR logs record transient “Connection reset by peer” exactly at that time, consistent with neighbors restarting.
- End-to-end tests between PCs succeed when run (initial reachability OK).

Mechanism: When FRR restarts, BGP adjacencies drop, advertised routes are withdrawn, and inter-subnet traffic (10.0.0.0/24 ↔ 10.0.1.0/24) briefly fails, appearing as intermittent connectivity. Localization: FRRouting daemons (bgpd/zebra) on all fabric routers, not physical links; leaf_router_0_0 is healthy.

Root cause: a one-time coordinated FRR daemon restart across the fabric (likely management/automation), not a failing switch.

Corrective fix: No hardware swap needed. Avoid unintended FRR restarts during business hours; keep watchfrr supervising daemons; if an external job triggered the reload, disable/reschedule it. Optionally enable BFD/GR to minimize any future reconvergence blips. I will continue monitoring for additional flaps.

per_axis.rationale: The report does not state pc_0_0->pc_0_1 has 0% loss or that leaf_router_0_0's BGP sessions have steady uptimes—instead it notes only ‘reachability OK’ and recent short uptimes from a FRR restart.

The agent's investigation log contains direct observations that support the conclusions: end-to-end reachability OK, BGP adjacencies in Established state with short uptimes, FRR/daemon start times aligned across routers, and interfaces up with no errors. A couple of specific log-phrase claims (e.g., an explicit ‘Connection reset by peer’ string) are not visible in the provided snippets, but the overall evidence justifies the inference that a coordinated FRR restart caused a transient, non-persistent disruption and that no hardware/switch failure is present.
